resources.string: Low-level switches for tracking down hardware trouble

Low-level switches for tracking down hardware trouble, mostly on clone consoles. Changes kick in right away and stick around after a restart. If the console fails to start twice in a row with tweaks on, they switch themselves off.
Nothing changed, everything is at the default
Off, everything runs at the default. Your choices are kept for when you switch this back on.
Switched off because the console didn\'t finish starting twice in a row. One of the tweaks is probably the reason. Switch this back on to try again.
What each setting does and why you\'d change it, right in the list
Back to the defaults for this console
Put every kernel tweak back to its default?
Safe: fine to try on any console
Last resort: try this only when nothing else helped
Risky: can stop things from working, you\'re on your own
Some changes only take effect after a restart.
Start option: %1$s (takes effect after a restart)
What the chip switches off while asleep, and the cores\' idle power-down
CPU, graphics and memory speeds are on the Performance page

Deep sleep hands the whole chip over to the firmware, which switches off almost everything. Light sleep just freezes the apps and lets the cores idle. The firmware isn\'t involved and no cores get switched off.
If your console freezes or restarts in sleep, try light sleep. It skips the part where these consoles get stuck. The catch: it drains the battery a lot faster, so it\'s more of a test than a fix.
Goes through the motions of falling asleep, but stops at the step you pick, waits 5 seconds and wakes up again. The console never actually sleeps while this is on.

Narrows down where sleep goes wrong. If \"Stop after switching cores off\" hangs, the problem is before the firmware. If everything works up to \"Stop right before sleeping\", it\'s the firmware or the hardware. Resets when the console restarts, so you can\'t get stuck with it.
How the console tells that a charger is plugged in. Most consoles have a pin that says so. On some clones that pin says \"plugged in\" all the time, so there the power chip has to see power as well.
If the console doesn\'t notice the charger, or shows \"charging\" with nothing plugged in, try the other setting. The default is picked for each console.

The power chip only takes a few input current limits (450, 850 or 1500 mA and more). Normally the console picks the step below what it asks for, so 800 mA becomes 450 mA. On picks the nearest step instead, so 800 mA becomes 850 mA. Takes effect the next time a charger is plugged in.
Try it if your console charges very slowly or not at all on a good charger. Off is how the console has always charged.
Normally the kernel stops writing its log the moment the drivers go to sleep. This keeps it writing right up to the last step.
When a console hangs in sleep, the problem report only shows what was logged before the hang. Keeping the log running shows more of the last steps. Sleep gets a tiny bit slower.
Writes a log line for every driver going to sleep and waking up, with how long it took.
Shows which driver was the last one before a hang, or which one makes waking up slow. Fills the log fast, so switch it off when you\'re done.
Logs the kernel\'s extra notes about sleep: which wakeup sources are active, why a sleep attempt gave up, and so on.
For when the console won\'t go to sleep at all, or wakes up again right away.
Switches processor cores off. The first core always stays on.

Some clones have a flaky core that hangs now and then. If the console gets steadier with fewer cores, that\'s your answer. Also means fewer cores to switch off on the way into sleep, which helps when testing sleep hangs. Games will run slower.
The chip temperature where the processor starts slowing down to cool off.

None of these consoles have any cooling, the chip is bare, so heavy games hit the limit fast and stutter. A heatsink or heat pad (a popular mod) helps the most. Raising the limit trades a hotter console for fewer slowdowns. Lowering it keeps the shell cooler. Above 90 °C isn\'t great for the chip in the long run.
Turns off the Performance overlay and the graphs in the power menu, and stops reading the numbers behind them (frame rate, CPU, temperature, battery, memory and SD card) in the background.
Saves the little bit of processor time the readings take, for squeezing out the last frames in a heavy game. Without it there are no numbers to see what a game is doing.
How eagerly Android moves idle apps into compressed memory (zram) to free up RAM.

Higher keeps more apps open in the background but costs a bit of processor time. Lower keeps things snappier while a game runs, but apps get closed sooner. On 1 GB consoles the default is usually best.
How quickly the kernel forgets which files and folders it looked at recently.
Lower makes browsing big ROM folders faster the second time round. Higher frees memory sooner for games.
How many pages the kernel pulls back out of compressed memory at once: 1, 2 or 8.
1 page is the usual choice for compressed memory and cuts small hitches when switching apps. More only helps with a real swap file, which these consoles don\'t have.
Whether the kernel sorts and groups reads and writes before sending them to the card, or just sends them in order.
Sorted keeps the system smooth while a big copy is running. \"As they come\" has less overhead and can be faster on good cards. On cheap or fake cards, sorted is usually the safer bet.
How much extra the kernel reads in one go when an app reads a file from start to end.

More read-ahead loads big ROMs and ISOs faster, especially from slow cards. Too much wastes memory and can slow down games that jump around in a file. If you swap the card, the setting is applied again at the next start.
Turns a stick direction around, on top of what this console\'s screen file already does.
Some clones wire a stick the other way round, so pushing right moves left or up moves down. Tick the direction that\'s backwards. Check in the controller test that it\'s right now.
Makes the left stick act as the right one and the right stick as the left one, pressing them in (L3/R3) too.
For clones with the sticks the wrong way round, or if you\'d rather steer with the other stick. Directions you flipped above stay with the stick you flipped them on.
How often the sticks are read and the buttons checked again.
Shorter means a little less input lag on the sticks but uses a bit more battery. Button presses come through right away anyway. Longer helps if the sticks jitter on a noisy clone.
Reads the headphone jack\'s switch the other way round.
Some clones wire the jack backwards: the speaker stays quiet with nothing plugged in, or sound never moves to the headphones. If that sounds like yours, flip it. It\'s checked again right away.
How much the kernel writes to the log that survives a crash or restart.
More detail means a better chance the line that explains a hang makes it into the problem report. \"Everything\" is very chatty and can slow the console down a bit.
How long the console waits after a kernel crash before it restarts by itself.

Restarting quickly gets you back to playing, and the problem report still has the crash log. \"Never\" keeps the console frozen so you can see that it crashed rather than hung, but you\'ll need to hold Power to switch it off.
When a driver hits a serious error (an oops), the kernel normally carries on without it. This restarts the console instead.
After an oops things often break in odd ways: no sound, dead buttons, a frozen screen later on. Restarting right away gets you a clean crash log in the problem report instead of a confusing mess.
How long a core can stop responding before the kernel logs a warning with what it was doing.
The sleep hangs on some clones look like one core going quiet. A shorter time gets that warning into the log before you give up and hold Power.
Lets the charger, battery gauge and sound parts of the power chip (RK817) log what they\'re doing.
For battery percentages that jump around, charging that stops or sound that crackles. Very chatty, so only switch it on while you\'re making a problem report.
Keeps a crash record when a driver hits a serious error (an oops) and the kernel carries on, not only when the whole kernel crashes.

An oops is often the start of trouble that shows up later: no sound, dead buttons, a frozen screen. With this on, the problem report after the next restart has it. Off saves only full kernel crashes, so a harmless oops doesn\'t bring up the crash notice after the next start.
Save the log at every restart
When the console restarts normally, the kernel also saves the end of its log in the crash record, with every message, also the quiet ones below the log level.

For problems without a crash, such as a game that stutters until you restart. The last start\'s kernel log is kept anyway, but only the lines at the log level. A crash in the same start always keeps its own record. A normal restart replaces an older crash record though, so save the problem report about a crash first. Nothing is kept after switching off: the RAM loses it.
Sends the kernel log out of the debug serial port and lets you type commands there (UART2 on the R36S, UART5 on EE clones).
Only useful with a USB serial adapter soldered to the board. Off by default: on some clones a floating serial pin wakes the console from sleep, and every log line costs a little time while it\'s on.
How much the kernel logs from the very first moment of a start, before Android is up. The \"Kernel log detail\" setting above only kicks in later.
For consoles that hang or restart while starting. With the serial console on, this is also what goes out of the serial port.
How much memory is set aside at start for the screen, graphics and video decoding (CMA). The rest is left for apps.
Less gives games and apps more room, which helps on 1 GB and 512 MB consoles. Too little and videos or some emulators fail to start. If that happens, go back to the default.
Lets idle cores go into a deeper power-saving state. Off keeps them in the lightest one.
If the console freezes randomly or in sleep, switching this off rules the idle states out. It costs some battery.
Whether the kernel\'s timer keeps ticking on idle cores, or pauses until there\'s work.
Pausing saves battery. Always running can smooth out stutter in some emulators and rules out timer trouble when chasing freezes. It costs some battery.
Logs how long each part of the kernel takes to start.
For finding what makes a start slow or where it hangs. Adds lots of lines to the log, so switch it off again once the problem report is made.
Lets USB devices (controllers, Wi-Fi sticks, keyboards) power down when they\'re not in use.
Some cheap USB controllers and Wi-Fi sticks drop out or lag after a pause. Off keeps them awake, at the cost of some battery.
Off keeps every Wi-Fi and Bluetooth driver from loading, for a chip built into the console and for USB sticks alike. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth don\'t work at all then.

For consoles with built-in Wi-Fi. On most of them the chip is wired to the USB port, and while its driver runs, USB OTG devices like controllers, sticks and keyboards don\'t work there. Off frees the port for OTG.

How apps reach the internal storage and the SD cards. sdcardfs hands every file read and write straight to the kernel. FUSE, Android\'s usual way, sends each one through the Media Storage app first, which costs CPU time and battery on this chip.

Leave it on sdcardfs unless an app has trouble with its files. Games, saves and downloads stay where they are either way. But the two modes mark the folders apps keep for themselves (Android/data) differently, so right after a switch an app may not be able to read its own settings or downloads. Android usually sorts this out by itself. If an app breaks or forgets its settings after you switch, switch back.
Off keeps the kernel\'s FUSE driver from starting, which saves about 100 KB of memory. With sdcardfs, Android doesn\'t need FUSE for storage.

Only worth it when every bit of memory counts. Android still uses FUSE for appfuse: opening files from a phone or camera connected over USB (MTP) in the Files app, and apps that hand out virtual files. Those fail while it\'s off. If something can\'t open files after you switch it off, switch it back on.

On switches on the eMMC storage chip some consoles have built in, from the next start, so a problem report can show what is on it: its size, partitions and their names. The kernel only reads it and refuses every write, so the system that came with the console stays as it is. It doesn\'t show up as storage or in the Files app.

A first look at the built-in storage, for installing andr36oid there one day. Only for consoles where its pins are free, the others don\'t have it. Experimental: if the console doesn\'t start with it on, the tweaks switch themselves off after two failed starts.
Stays on while the storage layer is FUSE: storage runs on it then.
Keeps the kernel log, the Android log and a crash record in a piece of RAM that survives a restart, so the next start can put them into the problem report.

Leave it on. Off is only for testing whether the crash log itself causes trouble. The problem report then lacks the log of the start before, and kernel crashes no longer bring up the crash notice. The 960 KB stay set aside anyway: the device tree reserves them, they just go unused.

How fast the console talks to its built-in eMMC, from the next start, when Built-in eMMC storage is on. High speed is what the system that came with the console uses. DDR52 sends data twice per clock tick, about twice as fast. HS200 runs the clock up to three times faster, on chips that have it; the others stay at DDR52.

Faster backups and, one day, a faster system on the eMMC. On the Diium D-28S, high speed reads about 40 MB/s, DDR52 about 75 MB/s and HS200 about 107 MB/s. If the eMMC doesn\'t show up or reads fail, pick a slower speed. The eMMC is only read, so a speed that doesn\'t work can\'t harm it.

How the 960 KB kept across a restart are shared between the crash record, the kernel log and the Android log. Balanced: 192 KB, 512 KB and 256 KB. More kernel log: 320 KB, 512 KB and 128 KB. More Android log: 192 KB, 256 KB and 512 KB.

Balanced suits most problems. More kernel log fits the whole kernel log into the crash record, for crashes with a long story before them. More Android log keeps twice as much of Android\'s log, for apps and games that close or freeze without a kernel crash. The logs from before the switch are lost at the restart that changes it.
